## The question, frozen

The document answers several questions. The title makes *Meno* central, and the dialogue's first line asks whether virtue comes "by teaching or by practice; or if neither... by nature, or in what other way." The introduction calls the whole piece "an attempt to answer the question, Can virtue be taught?" I take that as the frozen question: **how does virtue arrive in a person — can it be taught?** Range: the virtue of a man who runs a house or a state, in the Athens and Thessaly of the dialogue. Asked forward (what produces it?), though I note below that much of the argument answers a backward question instead. "What is virtue?" is treated in the text as a precondition of this question, so I carry it as a job, not as the question. Where the text drifts to "is there knowledge in the higher sense?", I record that as a new question, not a rescue.

## The explanation in parts, with a mark on each

| Part, in the text's words | Mark |
|---|---|
| "Do not suppose that we can explain... virtue as a whole through some unexplained portion of virtue" | **Held** — by the job of catching Meno's third definition, which repeats "justice", a part of virtue. The figure/colour drill ("whiteness is *a* colour, not colour") is the change that shows it working. |
| "Assume that if virtue is knowledge, then virtue can be taught" | **Fixed** — Socrates sets it "under an hypothesis, as mathematicians do". Everything drawn from it inherits that. |
| "Virtue is a good, and goods must be under the direction of knowledge" | **Held if** — held only on the assumption above. One case would break it: something known but not teachable. The text never runs that case. |
| "There are no teachers... the sons of great men were remarkable for riding and wrestling" | **Held if** — its job needs an added claim, that a father who *could* teach would have taught his son successfully. Swap in "the sons had it and wasted it", or a father too busy to teach, and the same fact survives. Poke that would matter and is never run: find one good son. |
| "Virtue is and is not teachable" | The **pull** between the two rows above; which one gives way is decided by the next row. |
| "In this higher and ideal sense there is no virtue and no knowledge" | **Fixed** — a limit set by the text and stated out loud, but carrying no reason inside the explanation for where the line falls. Swap "ideal" for "systematic and teachable": nothing in the document decides between them. |
| "Right opinion... is incapable of being taught... not bound by the tie of the cause" | **Held** — one poke does real work: ask the man who runs the state well to give his reason. No other part makes that difference. This is the part doing two jobs. |

| "No one desires evil" | **Loose, and the answer sits in the starting point.** "Good" slides from *what is good* to *what is desired*, so Meno's definition quietly becomes "the power of attaining it". | Meno as "a Thessalian Alcibiades"; Anytus as "the narrow-minded man of the world" | **Fixed** — the introduction's own reading of the characters, and in Meno's case expressly not the historical man. |

## Whole-explanation checks

**Direction.** The strongest argument is backward: from there being no remarkable sons, read off that there were no teachers. That answers "what can we tell from what we see?" The forward question — what produces virtue in a person — is not answered this way, and the text says so by leaving it open.

**Flip.** Had a statesman's son turned out good, the same argument would have said teachers exist. That half survives the flip, which is a point in its favour. The "divine" label does not.

**Answer hidden in the starting points.** Twice. "Good" carries "desired"; and "he must always have been either a man or not a man" hides the conclusion in a false pair.

**Catch-all.** "Right opinion", "inspiration", "the divine" is a bin that absorbs any statecraft outcome. Its gauge is the text's own: whether the man can give the cause. Without that reading, the bin swallows every job.

**Rivals.** "Virtue is teachable but the art has not yet been found" and "no teacher exists" fit every observation on the list. Nothing listed tells them apart, so at this level they are the same explanation. Meno's fourth branch — by nature — is never put on the list at all.

**Where the parts came from.** Fitted: the claims about the sons of famous Athenians (tuned to Athenian reputation). Built: the definition-and-circularity machinery, which catches Meno's answers. Asserted: the immortal soul, "from priests and priestesses" and Pindar.

## What would make it harder to vary

1. Run the missing change: name one person who acquired virtue and can say how, or one son of a good father who is good for the same reason. The text looks straight at where it would look, and stops.
2. Give the "right opinion" bin its gauge: one case of a state well run by a man who cannot give a cause, one of a man who can. That is the only place the argument touches something checkable.

## What this does not show

This marks the argument as it stands in this document. It does not decide whether virtue is teachable, and a loose part is not a false one. The historical claims stay borrowed.

## One next step

Take the "tie of the cause" and write down, before asking, what a statesman's "no, I cannot say why" would look like — then ask one.
